question: True or false: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the first Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
source_excerpt: constructed c. 2600 BC over approximately 26 years during the reign of Pharaoh Khufu in the Fourth Dynasty

extra.why_interesting: Players file Cleopatra and the pyramids together as 'ancient Egypt', so the pyramids feel like her neighbours; in fact they were older to her than she is to us.
extra.verification_notes: Cleopatra (d. 30 BC) is ~2,000 years from the 1969 Moon landing but ~2,570 years from the Great Pyramid (c. 2600 BC), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza.

explanation: The Great Pyramid was already about 2,500 years old when Cleopatra died in 30 BC, while the Moon landing came only about 2,000 years after her. To Cleopatra, the pyramids were more ancient than she is to us.

question: Julius Caesar is often wrongly called Rome's first emperor. Who actually holds that title, taking power in 27 BC?
source_excerpt: was the founder of the Roman Empire and the first Roman emperor from 27 BC until his death in AD 14.

extra.why_interesting: Most people instinctively name Julius Caesar as the first emperor, but he was assassinated before the Empire existed; the real answer is his adopted heir.
extra.verification_notes: Augustus is universally regarded as the first Roman emperor, taking the title/name in 27 BC (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus).

explanation: Caesar's great-nephew and adopted heir Octavian took the name Augustus and ruled for over forty years, founding the Roman Empire. The month of August is named after him.

question: In which year did the Spanish Armada sail against Elizabeth I's England, only to be scattered and defeated?
source_excerpt: On 21 July 1588 (N.S), the armada set sail from Lisbon and headed for the English Channel.

extra.why_interesting: Players know it happened under Elizabeth I but often cannot place it; the century-wide spread of options makes partial knowledge of the Tudor era enough to reason it out.
extra.verification_notes: The Spanish Armada sailed against England in 1588 and was defeated, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Armada; the other options are clearly wrong.

explanation: Philip II of Spain sent about 130 ships in 1588. English fireships, bad weather and a long detour around Scotland and Ireland destroyed much of the fleet.

question: Roughly how many soldiers did Napoleon lead into Russia in 1812, in the largest army Europe had ever seen?
source_excerpt: Napoleon's initial force upon entering Russia exceeded 450,000 men, over 150,000 horses, approximately 25,000 wagons, and nearly 1,400 artillery pieces.

extra.why_interesting: The 1812 invasion was the largest army Europe had ever seen; players tend to think of armies of the era in tens of thousands and underestimate by a full order of magnitude.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia gives the initial Grande Armée crossing the Neman as roughly 440,000-450,000 men, which fits 'hundreds of thousands' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_invasion_of_Russia).

explanation: Over 600,000 men crossed into Russia in June 1812. After the retreat from Moscow, through winter cold, hunger and disease, only a few tens of thousands came back.

question: The wheel at the centre of India's national flag takes its name from which ancient Indian emperor?
source_excerpt: The spinning wheel of the Congress flag was replaced by the Ashoka Chakra from the Lion Capital of Ashoka.

extra.why_interesting: A symbol seen by over a billion people daily traces back to a ruler who died more than 2,200 years ago; players who know Indian history can connect the wheel to its Buddhist convert emperor.
extra.verification_notes: The wheel on India's flag is the Ashoka Chakra, taken from the Lion Capital of Ashoka (Emperor Ashoka, Maurya dynasty), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_India.

explanation: The Ashoka Chakra comes from the Lion Capital that the Mauryan emperor Ashoka erected at Sarnath in the third century BC. The same lion capital is India's national emblem.

question: Winston Churchill is the only British prime minister to have won a Nobel Prize. In which category did he win it?
source_excerpt: The Nobel Prize in Literature 1953 was awarded to Sir Winston Leonard Spencer Churchill "for his mastery of historical and biographical description as well as for brilliant oratory in defending exalted human values."

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a wartime leader's Nobel would be the Peace Prize; Churchill never won that one, but he did win for his writing and speeches.
extra.verification_notes: Churchill won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature and no other British PM has won a Nobel (https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/1953/churchill/documentary/).

explanation: Churchill received the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature for his historical writing and his speeches. He was nominated for the Peace Prize but never won it.

question: In 1698, Russia's Tsar Peter the Great imposed a special tax on men who refused to give up what?
source_excerpt: In 1698, Tsar Peter I of Russia instituted a beard tax as part of an effort to bring Russian society in line with Western European models.

extra.why_interesting: Taxes are supposed to target wealth or goods, so a tax on a man's face sounds like a joke; it was a real policy to force Russian nobles to look like Western Europeans.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia says Peter I instituted a beard tax in 1698, though formal decree and collection date to 1705; the answer 'beards' is correct.

explanation: Peter wanted Russians to look like clean-shaven Western Europeans. Men who paid the tax received a token proving they had bought the right to keep their beard.

question: Abraham Lincoln was shot in 1865 while watching a play at Ford's Theatre. What was the profession of his assassin, John Wilkes Booth?
source_excerpt: John Wilkes Booth (May 10, 1838 – April 26, 1865) was an American stage actor who assassinated United States president Abraham Lincoln at Ford's Theatre

extra.why_interesting: The assassin was not a soldier or a stranger but a celebrity performer, which is exactly why he could move freely around the theatre where Lincoln sat.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia describes Booth as an American stage actor who assassinated Lincoln at Ford's Theatre in 1865: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wilkes_Booth

explanation: Booth came from a famous theatrical family and had performed at Ford's Theatre himself, so he knew the building and nobody questioned his presence backstage.

question: Russia's empress Catherine the Great was not Russian by birth. Her birthplace lies in which present-day country?
source_excerpt: Catherine was born on 2 May 1729 as Princess Sophie Auguste Friederike von Anhalt-Zerbst-Dornburg, in the city of Stettin (now known as Szczecin)

extra.why_interesting: Players who know she was a German princess confidently answer 'Germany', but her Prussian birthplace has been Polish since 1945, so the modern-borders framing flips the expected answer.
extra.verification_notes: Catherine was born in Stettin, Prussia, now Szczecin, Poland, so the answer holds (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_the_Great).

explanation: She was born a German princess in Stettin, then part of Prussia. After the Second World War the city became Szczecin in Poland, so her birthplace is now Polish, not German.

question: After his release from a Communist prison in 1959, China's last emperor Puyi took an ordinary job in Beijing. What did he do for a living?
source_excerpt: he worked as a gardener before he became a researcher at the Central Research Institute of Culture and History

extra.why_interesting: A man who had been worshipped as Son of Heaven ended up tending plants for a wage; the contrast between throne and flowerbed is the whole payoff.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Puyi worked as a gardener after his 1959 release, before later becoming a researcher (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puyi).

explanation: Puyi worked at the Beijing Botanical Gardens, sweeping and tending plants. Later he was given a research post, and he died in 1967 as an ordinary citizen.

question: In 1532, Francisco Pizarro and fewer than 200 Spaniards ambushed and captured the ruler of the Inca Empire. Who was that emperor?
source_excerpt: the ambush and seizure of the Incan ruler Atahualpa by a small Spanish force led by Francisco Pizarro

extra.why_interesting: Most players know Cortés and Moctezuma but blank on the Inca equivalent; the tiny Spanish force seizing the ruler of the largest empire in the Americas is one of history's most lopsided ambushes.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Battle of Cajamarca article confirms Pizarro's small force (106 infantry plus 62 cavalry) ambushed and captured Atahualpa in 1532.

explanation: Atahualpa was seized at Cajamarca while thousands of his unarmed attendants were cut down. He paid a vast ransom in gold and silver, but the Spanish executed him anyway the following year.

question: The Holy Roman Empire was founded with Charlemagne's coronation in the year 800. In which year was it formally dissolved?
source_excerpt: Emperor Francis II abdicated and formally dissolved the empire following the creation by French emperor Napoleon of the Confederation of the Rhine.

extra.why_interesting: Most players file the Holy Roman Empire under the Middle Ages and are startled that it survived into the age of steam engines, falling only when Napoleon pushed it over.
extra.verification_notes: The empire was formally dissolved on 6 August 1806 per Wikipedia; the 800 founding premise is debated (800/962) but doesn't affect the answer.

explanation: Emperor Francis II abdicated in August 1806 after Napoleon crushed Austria at Austerlitz and gathered the German states into his own Confederation of the Rhine. An empire that had outlasted the Vikings, the Black Death and the Reformation was ended by a Corsican in his thirties.

question: In 1896 Britain fought the shortest war in recorded history, over in under an hour, against the sultanate of which East African island?
source_excerpt: The conflict lasted between 38 and 45 minutes, marking it as the shortest recorded war in history.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture wars lasting years; learning that one ended before the tea went cold, and that it was fought over a disputed succession on a spice island, is the kind of absurd detail that sticks. The stem's footholds (1896, Britain, East African island sultanate) let a reasoning player land on Zanzibar.
extra.verification_notes: Anglo-Zanzibar War of 27 Aug 1896 lasted 38-45 minutes and is recorded as the shortest war in history; Zanzibar is an island sultanate.

explanation: The Anglo-Zanzibar War lasted roughly forty minutes: British warships bombarded the palace after a disputed succession, and the new sultan fled before lunch.

question: Alexander the Great died in 323 BC aged just 32, in which ancient Mesopotamian city, famed for its hanging gardens?
source_excerpt: later died in 323 BC in Babylon, Mesopotamia, the city which he had planned to make the capital of his empire, while on his return to Greece.

extra.why_interesting: Most people know Alexander as a world conqueror but assume a long reign; the shock is that he was dead at 32, and in a city he had taken rather than one he built. The 'hanging gardens' foothold gives a reasoning player a route to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BC aged 32; Babylon is famed for the Hanging Gardens.

explanation: He fell ill at the palace of Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon and died within about two weeks, leaving no clear heir and an empire that his generals immediately carved up.

question: Which gymnast scored the first perfect 10 in Olympic history, at the 1976 Games?
source_excerpt: she was awarded the first perfect 10 in Olympic gymnastics for her routine on the uneven bars.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a perfect 10 was always part of gymnastics; in fact it was so unthinkable that the scoreboard literally could not display it.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Comăneci received the first perfect 10 in Olympic gymnastics on July 18, 1976; a 'first' claim cannot be overtaken by later events.

explanation: She was 14, and the Montreal scoreboard had only three digits, so her historic 10.00 flashed up as 1.00.

question: True or false: a modern Olympic gold medal is made of solid gold.
source_excerpt: composed at least 92.5% of silver, plated with 6 grams of gold.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone pictures a lump of pure gold around the champion's neck; it is actually a silver medal wearing a thin gold coat.
extra.verification_notes: Olympic gold medals are at least 92.5% silver with a minimum of 6 g of gold plating, not solid gold; the last solid gold medals were in 1912 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_medal).

explanation: The last solid gold medals were handed out in 1912; today's are mostly silver with a coating of about six grams of gold.

question: In darts, what is the highest score possible with a single throw of three darts?
source_excerpt: The highest score possible with three darts is 180, commonly known as a 'ton 80' ... obtained when all three darts land in the triple 20.

extra.why_interesting: Even non-players have heard the crowd roar 'one hundred and eighty', and the number can be reasoned out from the board: 20 is the top segment and the treble ring triples it.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms 180 (three treble 20s) is the maximum score with three darts; no newer development changes this.

explanation: Three darts in the treble 20 bed score 60 each, and the referee's shout of 'one hundred and eighty' is the sport's signature moment.

question: In which year were the first Winter Olympic Games held, in Chamonix, France?
source_excerpt: decided to retrospectively grant the Chamonix competitions the status of the first Winter Olympic Games

extra.why_interesting: The Summer Games began in 1896, so players expect the Winter Games to be a near contemporary; in fact they came almost three decades later.
extra.verification_notes: The first Winter Olympics were held in Chamonix in 1924, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1924_Winter_Olympics.

explanation: The 1924 Chamonix event was originally billed as an 'International Winter Sports Week' and only retroactively named the first Winter Olympics.

question: Which NBA player scored 100 points in a single game in 1962, a record that still stands?
source_excerpt: Wilt Chamberlain scored 100 points for the Philadelphia Warriors against the New York Knicks on March 2, 1962

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a modern superstar like Kobe or Jordan owns the scoring record; it has belonged to one man since 1962 and nobody has come within a dozen points.
extra.verification_notes: Chamberlain scored 100 on March 2, 1962 and the record remains unbroken; the nearest recent attempt was 83 points (Bam Adebayo, March 2026), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilt_Chamberlain%27s_100-point_game

explanation: He did it for the Philadelphia Warriors in a small arena in Hershey, Pennsylvania, with no television cameras present, so only a famous photo of him holding a '100' sign survives.

question: The Tour de France leader wears a yellow jersey because the race's founding organiser was what kind of business?
source_excerpt: the man leading the race should wear a jersey in the colours of L'Auto.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the colour was chosen for visibility or glory; it was actually an advertisement for a newspaper's distinctive paper.
extra.verification_notes: The Tour was founded by the newspaper L'Auto, printed on yellow paper, and the yellow jersey matched its colours, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_jersey.

explanation: The sports paper L'Auto created the race in 1903 and printed on yellow paper, so when the leader's jersey arrived in 1919 it matched the pages.

question: In chess, how many different legal moves can White choose from for the very first move of the game?
source_excerpt: Number of plies (half-moves) | Number of possible games | 1 | 20

extra.why_interesting: Players imagine a huge number, then realise only pawns and knights can move and the count falls out neatly: eight pawns with two choices each, two knights with two each.
extra.verification_notes: White has 20 legal first moves (16 pawn moves and 4 knight moves), which matches the table of possible games after 1 ply at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shannon_number.

explanation: Only the pawns and knights can move at the start: eight pawns can go one or two squares, and each knight has two landing squares, making 16 plus 4.

question: The street names on the original American Monopoly board, such as Boardwalk and Park Place, come from which seaside city?
source_excerpt: The original version of the game in this format was based on the streets of Atlantic City, New Jersey.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the board is an invented or generic city, or guess New York; it is in fact a map of a seaside resort town.
extra.verification_notes: Monopoly's original street names come from Atlantic City, NJ, per Wikipedia; Marvin Gardens' Margate origin is a minor quirk that doesn't create a second defensible answer.

explanation: The 1930s board copied real streets from the New Jersey resort, and most of them, including Boardwalk, still exist today.

question: Roughly how many dimples are there on a standard golf ball?
source_excerpt: Most modern golf balls have about 300–500 dimples

extra.why_interesting: The ball looks smooth from a distance and people guess a few dozen, but anyone who has held one can picture the dense pattern and reason their way to hundreds.
extra.verification_notes: Standard golf balls have roughly 300-500 dimples (e.g. Pro V1 352), so 'Hundreds' is correct per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf_ball.

explanation: Most balls carry between 300 and 500 dimples, which reduce drag and let a ball fly nearly twice as far as a smooth one would.

question: At the 1956 Melbourne Olympics, one entire sport was instead held in Stockholm, months earlier and on the other side of the world. Which sport?
source_excerpt: The competitions were held from 11 to 17 June 1956 at Stockholm Olympic Stadium.

extra.why_interesting: Splitting an Olympics across two hemispheres sounds absurd until the player asks what Australia is famously strict about: bringing in animals.
extra.verification_notes: All 1956 Olympic equestrian events were held in Stockholm 11-17 June because of Australian quarantine rules, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equestrian_at_the_1956_Summer_Olympics

explanation: Australia's quarantine rules would have kept the horses isolated for months, so the riding events moved to Sweden and the Games were split across two continents.

question: In 1939, a cricket Test match between South Africa and England was abandoned as a draw after nine days of play. What did the England team have to leave to catch?
source_excerpt: abandoned as a draw after nine days of play spread over twelve days, otherwise the England team would have missed the boat for home.

extra.why_interesting: A match designed to be played to a finish still ended without a result, and the reason is wonderfully mundane: 1939 travel had a fixed timetable.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1939 Durban Test was abandoned as a draw after nine days so England could catch their ship home.

explanation: It was a 'timeless' Test meant to be played to a finish, but after nine days England had to take the train to Cape Town for the boat back to Britain, and no Test has been played without a time limit since.

question: In snooker, what is the score of a maximum break, the highest possible from a normal starting position?
source_excerpt: A break of up to 155 is possible if the referee awards a free ball before any of the reds have been potted.

extra.why_interesting: The odd-looking number is derived from the rules, and a player who knows reds are worth one and the black seven can build it: 15 times 8 plus the 27 points of the colours.
extra.verification_notes: 147 is the maximum break from a normal start (15 reds+blacks = 120, plus 27 for colours); the 155 free-ball case is excluded by the 'normal starting position' wording. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_break

explanation: Fifteen reds each followed by a black give 120 points, and clearing the six colours adds 27 more, a feat first achieved in professional play by Steve Davis in 1982.

question: In Mexico City in 1968, an American athlete's mark went so far beyond the optical measuring device's range that officials had to fetch a tape measure. His result is still the Olympic record today. In which event?
source_excerpt: is still the Olympic record and the second-longest in history unassisted by wind

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes Olympic records in explosive events get rewritten every few Games; the idea that one 1968 mark literally broke the measuring equipment and still tops the Olympic list more than half a century later is startling.
extra.verification_notes: Beamon's 8.90 m long jump from 1968 is still the Olympic record; the optical-device and tape-measure detail comes from the well-known account and was not checked against a source.

explanation: Bob Beamon's 8.90 metres beat the existing world record by 55 centimetres, stood as the world record for almost 23 years, and no one has matched it at an Olympics since.

question: Boxing gold in 1920, bobsleigh gold in 1932. Who is the only person to have won Olympic gold at both the Summer and Winter Games in two different sports?
source_excerpt: the only one to have won gold in each in different events

extra.why_interesting: Players assume Summer and Winter champions live in completely separate worlds; the combination of boxing and bobsleigh, twelve years apart, sounds invented until you learn one man did both.
extra.verification_notes: Eagan (boxing 1920, bobsleigh 1932) remains the only person with golds in different sports at both Summer and Winter Games; Grafström's golds were all figure skating, so he doesn't qualify.

explanation: American Eddie Eagan took the light heavyweight boxing title in Antwerp, then rode the four-man bobsleigh to victory in Lake Placid twelve years later, a double nobody has matched since.

question: The longest-standing individual world record in athletics was set in Munich in 1983 by a Czechoslovak runner and has never been beaten. Over which distance?
source_excerpt: Kratochvílová holds the women's 800 meters world record at 1:53.28, set in 1983, a mark that remains the fastest ever recorded in the event.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume athletics records fall every few years with better shoes, tracks and science, yet the oldest individual mark on the books is a middle-distance time from 1983 that no woman has touched in over four decades.
extra.verification_notes: Kratochvílová's 1:53.28 800m record from Munich 1983 still stands as of Oct 2026 (Werro's 1:53.70 in Aug 2026 came closest) per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/800_metres.

explanation: Jarmila Kratochvílová ran 800 metres in 1 minute 53.28 seconds, and more than forty years later nobody has gone faster.

question: The Jordan River pours ordinary fresh water into the Dead Sea every day, yet the Dead Sea is roughly ten times saltier than the ocean. How does a lake fed by fresh water end up that salty?
correct_answer: No outlet; evaporation leaves the salt behind
alternative_answers: It is a terminal lake with no river flowing out
Water only leaves by evaporation, so minerals accumulate
Closed basin, salts concentrate over time
The inflow brings small amounts of salt that never leave
It is a lake with no drainage, so salt builds up
headline_answer: No outlet; evaporation leaves the salt behind
source_excerpt: makes it approximately 9.6 times as salty as the ocean

extra.verification_notes: The Dead Sea is endorheic with no outlet, and evaporation concentrates the salts; salinity is about 9.6 times the ocean's, per Wikipedia.

explanation: The Dead Sea sits at the lowest point on Earth's land surface, so water flows in but has no river flowing out. In the hot desert climate the only way water leaves is by evaporating, and evaporation removes pure water while every dissolved mineral the river carried stays in the basin. Over thousands of years those traces have concentrated into brine of around 34 percent salinity, dense enough that swimmers float effortlessly. Any closed-basin lake in a dry climate ends up the same way, which is why the Great Salt Lake in Utah and Lake Urmia in Iran are also hypersaline.

question: Africa's highest mountain rises in which country?
source_excerpt: Mount Kilimanjaro is a large dormant stratovolcano in Tanzania. It is the highest mountain in Africa

extra.why_interesting: Many players associate Kilimanjaro with Kenya because of safari imagery and the classic view from Amboseli; the summit is actually on the Tanzanian side.
extra.verification_notes: Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain, is in Tanzania, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kilimanjaro).

explanation: Kilimanjaro tops out at roughly 5,895 metres, and although the famous postcard view is from Kenya's Amboseli park, the whole mountain lies inside Tanzania.

question: The lowest point on dry land anywhere on Earth sits on the shore of which body of water?
topic: Physical geography of the Middle East
source_excerpt: making its shores the lowest land-based elevation on Earth

extra.why_interesting: The Dead Sea is famous for floating and salt, but fewer players connect it with being the lowest spot on the planet's land surface.
extra.verification_notes: Dead Sea shores are the lowest exposed land elevation on Earth; subglacial Antarctic trenches are ice-covered, not dry land (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea).

explanation: Its shoreline lies roughly 430 metres below sea level, and the lake keeps dropping by about a metre a year as inflow from the Jordan River shrinks.

question: Which city is the northernmost national capital of a sovereign country?
source_excerpt: Northernmost capital of an independent sovereign state in the world.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Oslo, Helsinki or Moscow before remembering that Iceland's capital sits just below the Arctic Circle, further north than all of them.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's list of national capitals by latitude names Reykjavík as the northernmost capital of an independent sovereign state; Nuuk and Longyearbyen are in non-sovereign territories.

explanation: Iceland's capital sits at about 64 degrees north, well beyond Helsinki or Oslo, and only Greenland's Nuuk lies further north among capitals, but Greenland is not a sovereign state.

question: Bolivia's government sits in La Paz, but which city does the country's constitution name as its capital?
source_excerpt: As designated in the Constitution of Bolivia, Sucre is the true capital of the nation, while La Paz is the seat of government.

extra.why_interesting: Nearly everyone names La Paz, but Bolivia's constitution still names a different, smaller city as the capital.
extra.verification_notes: Sucre is the constitutional capital of Bolivia and La Paz is the seat of government; no recent change found (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucre).

explanation: Sucre has been Bolivia's official capital since independence and still hosts the Supreme Court, while the president and parliament moved to La Paz in the late nineteenth century.

question: By longitude, one US state is both the westernmost and the easternmost in the country. Which state?
source_excerpt: Pochnoi Point, Semisopochnoi Island, Alaska – easternmost point in all U.S. territory by longitude

extra.why_interesting: Players look for an east-coast state, but the trick is that one state's islands stretch past the antimeridian, making it the most eastern by longitude too.
extra.verification_notes: Alaska's Semisopochnoi Island lies at 179°46′E, past the 180th meridian, so Alaska has both the westernmost and easternmost points by longitude (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_points_of_the_United_States).

explanation: Alaska's Aleutian Islands run so far west that they cross the 180th meridian, so their far end technically lies in the Eastern Hemisphere, east of every other state.

question: Everest is the highest peak above sea level, but the mountaintop farthest from the centre of the Earth stands in which country?
source_excerpt: the farthest point on the surface from Earth's center, with Huascarán in Peru a very close second.

extra.why_interesting: Everest wins on height above sea level, but Earth bulges at the equator, so a lower volcano near the equator actually sticks out farther into space.
extra.verification_notes: Chimborazo (Ecuador) is widely reported as the farthest point from Earth's centre; Huascarán (Peru) is a very close second, within measurement error, but the standard answer holds.

explanation: Earth bulges at the equator, so the summit of Chimborazo, just one degree south of it, is about 2 kilometres farther from the planet's centre than Everest's.

question: Three of these Central European countries are landlocked. Which one has a sea coast?
source_excerpt: its southwestern boundary consists of a 46.6-kilometre (29.0 mi) coastline on the Adriatic Sea.

extra.why_interesting: Four small Central European countries look alike on the surface, and only a player who pictures the top of the Adriatic knows which one actually touches the sea.
extra.verification_notes: Slovenia has a 46.6 km Adriatic coastline, while Austria, Hungary and Slovakia are landlocked (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovenia).

explanation: Slovenia squeezes in about 47 kilometres of Adriatic coastline between Italy and Croatia, with the port of Koper, while the other three have no sea at all.

question: True or false: measured from east to west, mainland Australia is wider than the diameter of the Moon.
source_excerpt: the straight-line distance between the east and west is 4,030 km, measured between Steep Point and Cape Byron

extra.why_interesting: The Moon feels like a whole world and Australia like one country, yet the continent is wider than the Moon is across.
extra.verification_notes: Mainland Australia's east-west extent is ~4,030 km (Steep Point to Cape Byron), exceeding the Moon's ~3,475 km diameter; https://www.ga.gov.au/scientific-topics/national-location-information/dimensions/continental-extremities

explanation: Australia stretches close to 4,000 kilometres from coast to coast, while the Moon measures only about 3,470 kilometres across.

question: Which city lies further north: Rome or New York City?

extra.why_interesting: Players picture sunny Mediterranean Rome and snowy New York, so the latitude ordering feels backwards until they remember the Gulf Stream warms Europe.
extra.verification_notes: Rome is at 41.89°N versus New York City at 40.71°N, so Rome lies further north (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome).

explanation: Rome sits at nearly 42 degrees north, over a hundred kilometres further north than New York, but the warm Mediterranean and Atlantic currents give it the milder winters.

question: Which river flows through four national capital cities, more than any other river on Earth?
source_excerpt: four national capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade

extra.why_interesting: Players assume capitals sit on their own separate rivers; realising one river strings together four capitals in a row is a small 'of course' moment, and the Danube is familiar enough that most players can reach it.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Danube flows through four national capitals (Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, Belgrade), and I know of no other river that passes through as many, though the article doesn't state the comparison.

explanation: On its way from Germany to the Black Sea the Danube passes Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade, and touches ten countries in total, also a world record.

question: Sweden has more islands than any other country on Earth. Roughly how many does it have?
source_excerpt: Sweden has approximately 267,570 islands

extra.why_interesting: Players think of island nations like Indonesia or the Philippines, which have tens of thousands, and would never guess a mainland Nordic country tops them with more than a quarter of a million.
extra.verification_notes: Sweden is ranked first with about 267,570 islands (SCB), so 'About 250,000' is the best option; no newer data contradicts it.

explanation: Statistics Sweden counts around 267,000 islands, most of them tiny rocky islets in lakes and along the coast, and fewer than a thousand are inhabited.

question: Which landlocked kingdom is the only country in the world whose entire territory lies more than 1,000 metres above sea level?
source_excerpt: It is the only independent state in the world that lies entirely above 1,000 metres (3,281 ft) in elevation.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Nepal, Bhutan or Switzerland, all of which have valleys far below 1,000 metres; the real answer is a small African kingdom they rarely think of, and the 'landlocked kingdom' foothold leaves exactly one candidate.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Lesotho is the only independent state entirely above 1,000 m (lowest point 1,400 m) and is a landlocked kingdom.

explanation: Lesotho's lowest point is about 1,400 metres up, the highest low point of any country, which is why it is nicknamed the Kingdom in the Sky.

question: Even very ticklish people cannot tickle themselves, no matter how hard they try. What is it about the brain that makes self-tickling fail?
correct_answer: Brain predicts and cancels self-made touch
alternative_answers: The brain knows the touch is coming
Expected touch is dampened by the brain
You know where and when the touch will land
headline_answer: Brain predicts and cancels self-made touch
source_excerpt: The more participants attenuate the perception of their self-generated touch, the stronger the functional connectivity between the cerebellum and the somatosensory cortical areas

extra.verification_notes: Cerebellar forward-model prediction attenuating self-generated touch is the standard explanation (Blakemore et al.; PMC6975290).

explanation: When you move your own hand, the brain sends a copy of the motor command to the cerebellum, which forecasts the sensation that touch will produce. Because the prediction matches what arrives, the sensory signal is dampened before it reaches full awareness. Tickling relies on unpredictability, so a touch the brain already expected feels dull. When another person tickles you, there is no motor command to predict from, so the sensation arrives at full strength. Studies by Blakemore, Wolpert and Frith in 1998 even showed that a robot arm introducing a small random delay made self-tickling work again.

question: The smallest bone in the human body is about the size of a grain of rice. In which part of the body is it found?
source_excerpt: The stapes is the smallest and lightest bone in the human body

extra.why_interesting: Players picture bones as structural supports in limbs and fingers; the smallest one lives somewhere they never think of as having bones at all.
extra.verification_notes: The stapes in the middle ear is the smallest bone in the human body, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stapes; I found no newer developments that change this.

explanation: It is the stapes, or stirrup bone, deep in the middle ear, barely 3 millimetres long. Together with two neighbours it passes vibrations from the eardrum inward.

question: A giraffe's neck is about two metres long, yet it contains exactly the same number of vertebrae as your own neck. How many is that?
source_excerpt: Giraffes have seven neck vertebrae – the same number of neck bones that humans have.

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes a two-metre giraffe neck must contain far more bones than a human neck; it contains exactly the same number.
extra.verification_notes: Giraffes and humans both have seven cervical vertebrae; the roughly 2 m neck length is also accurate (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/giraffes-neck-bones-humans/).

explanation: Nearly every mammal, from a mouse to a giraffe, has seven neck vertebrae. The giraffe simply stretches each one to around 25 centimetres.

question: Every bone in the human skeleton connects to at least one other bone, with a single exception that floats in the throat, held only by muscles. Which bone is it?
source_excerpt: It is the only bone in the human body that is not connected to any other bones.

extra.why_interesting: A skeleton is imagined as one connected frame; one bone floats free, anchored only by soft tissue, and it is essential for speech and swallowing.
extra.verification_notes: The hyoid is widely recognised as the only bone that does not articulate with another bone; 'only by muscles' is a slight simplification since ligaments also anchor it.

explanation: The horseshoe-shaped hyoid sits above the voice box, anchoring the tongue and larynx. Its free-floating position is why forensic examiners check it for fractures in suspected strangulation.

question: Surgeons can remove up to two-thirds of this human organ and it will regrow to roughly its full size within months. Which organ?
source_excerpt: Only 10% of the original liver mass is required for the organ to regenerate back to full size.

extra.why_interesting: Humans are assumed to be poor at regrowing anything; one major organ can rebuild most of itself, which is what makes living-donor transplants possible.
extra.verification_notes: The liver regenerates to roughly full size after resection of up to two-thirds, per Wikipedia's liver regeneration article; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: This regrowth is what allows a living donor to give part of their liver to a patient, after which both portions grow back. The ancient Greeks may have known it too: Prometheus's punishment was an eagle eating his liver, which regrew each night.

question: One part of the human eye contains no blood vessels at all and absorbs its oxygen directly from the air. Which part?
source_excerpt: the healthy cornea does not have or need blood vessels within it.

extra.why_interesting: Every living tissue is assumed to be fed by blood; one transparent tissue has no blood supply at all, because blood vessels would block the view.
extra.verification_notes: The cornea is avascular and receives oxygen dissolved from the tear film/air; the lens is also avascular but is nourished by aqueous humor, so the answer is unambiguous (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornea).

explanation: Blood vessels would cloud the clear front window of the eye, so the cornea breathes through the tear film instead. That is also why wearing contact lenses too long can starve it of oxygen.

question: Your right lung has three lobes, but your left lung has only two and is noticeably smaller. Which organ is the reason it had to make room?
source_excerpt: The left lung shares space with the heart, and has an indentation in its border called the cardiac notch of the left lung to accommodate this.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the body is symmetrical; the lungs are not, and the reason is a neighbour they know well once they think about it.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the left lung has two lobes, is smaller than the right, and has a cardiac notch to accommodate the heart.

explanation: The heart sits slightly left of centre, with a notch in the left lung carved out to fit around it. The right lung compensates by being larger and heavier.

question: In 1980 the World Health Organization declared a disease eradicated worldwide, the only human disease ever wiped out completely. Which disease?
source_excerpt: Two infectious diseases have successfully been eradicated: smallpox in humans, and rinderpest in ruminants.

extra.why_interesting: Medicine has defeated many diseases in the public imagination, yet exactly one human disease has actually been wiped from the planet.
extra.verification_notes: Smallpox was declared eradicated by WHO in 1980 and remains the only eradicated human disease as of 2026 (rinderpest is animal-only; guinea worm and polio not yet eradicated), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eradication_of_infectious_diseases.

explanation: The last natural case was recorded in Somalia in 1977 after a global vaccination campaign. Only two laboratories, in the United States and Russia, still hold samples of the virus.

question: The painkiller aspirin was developed from a compound found in the bark of which tree, chewed for pain relief since ancient Greece?
source_excerpt: A precursor compound called salicin, found in willow tree bark, is metabolized into salicylic acid and has been used for its health effects for at least 2,400 years.

extra.why_interesting: Aspirin feels like a purely synthetic laboratory product, yet its chemistry comes from a tree that Hippocrates was already prescribing.
extra.verification_notes: Aspirin derives from salicin found in willow (Salix) bark, used medicinally since classical antiquity per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspirin; the 'chewed' detail is loose but not wrong.

explanation: Willow bark contains salicin, which chemists at Bayer turned into acetylsalicylic acid in the 1890s. Hippocrates recommended willow leaf tea for pain more than two thousand years earlier.

question: Which metal, bound inside the haemoglobin of your red blood cells, carries oxygen and gives human blood its red colour?
source_excerpt: A heme group consists of an iron (Fe) ion held in a heterocyclic ring, known as a porphyrin.

extra.why_interesting: The player knows blood is red and that anaemia involves a metal, but may not connect the two; the metal in their blood is the same one that rusts red.
extra.verification_notes: Heme iron in haemoglobin binds oxygen and is the only metal involved; the colour nuance (porphyrin ring) doesn't create another defensible answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemoglobin).

explanation: An adult body holds roughly four grams of iron, most of it in the blood. Horseshoe crabs use copper instead, which is why their blood is blue.

question: True or false: an adult is measurably taller when they wake up in the morning than when they go to bed at night.
source_excerpt: Quantitative Assessment of Intervertebral Disc Composition by MRI: Sensitivity to Diurnal Variation

extra.why_interesting: Height feels like a fixed number; in reality it changes measurably every single day, and the player's own spine is the mechanism.
extra.verification_notes: Well-established diurnal height variation of roughly 0.6–2 cm from spinal disc compression and rehydration; no newer findings contradict it (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10204382/).

explanation: True. The cushioning discs between your vertebrae compress by one to two centimetres over a day of standing and sitting, then re-expand while you lie down overnight.

question: Before this breakthrough in Toronto, a child diagnosed with type 1 diabetes rarely survived more than a couple of years. In which year was insulin first injected into a human patient?
source_excerpt: At Toronto General Hospital on 11 January 1922, house physician Ed Jeffrey injected Leonard Thompson with a beef-pancreas extract prepared by Frederick Banting and Charles Best.

extra.why_interesting: Diabetes is ancient and insulin feels like old medicine, yet before the 1920s a childhood diagnosis of type 1 diabetes was a death sentence within a year or two.
extra.verification_notes: Leonard Thompson received the first human insulin injection on 11 January 1922 at Toronto General Hospital (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Thompson_(diabetic)).

explanation: Fourteen-year-old Leonard Thompson received the first injection in January 1922, after Frederick Banting and Charles Best isolated insulin the previous year. Banting shared a Nobel Prize for it just one year later, in 1923.

question: A resting heart beats around 70 times a minute. Over an 80-year lifetime, roughly how many times does a human heart beat?
source_excerpt: How Many Times Does Your Heart Beat in a Lifetime? (2.5 Billion — Exact Math)

extra.why_interesting: The player can estimate from a familiar pulse rate but tends to stop a factor of ten short; the true lifetime total lands in the billions.
extra.verification_notes: 70 bpm × 80 years ≈ 2.94 billion beats, so 'Billions' is correct; sources cite ~2.5–3 billion (https://easetoolz.com/blog/heartbeat-in-a-lifetime).

explanation: Seventy beats a minute adds up to about 100,000 a day, 37 million a year, and close to 3 billion over 80 years. The heart does all of that without ever taking a day off.

question: Which organ in the human digestive system, despite its name, stretches to around six metres in length?
source_excerpt: The small intestine is about 6.5 metres (21 feet) long and folds many times to fit in the abdomen.

extra.why_interesting: Players hear 'small' and assume it is the short one; the answer flips that, and the explanation resolves it by revealing the name describes width, not length.
extra.verification_notes: Small intestine is commonly cited as ~6 m (6.5 m in cadavers, shorter in living people), and no other digestive organ with a misleading name approaches this length; source https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_intestine

explanation: The small intestine is about four times longer than the large intestine; it is called small because it is narrower, not shorter.

question: Tetris was created in 1984 by a programmer working at a state academy of sciences in which country?
source_excerpt: Dorodnitsyn Computing Center of the Academy of Sciences in the Soviet Union

extra.why_interesting: One of the most Western-feeling, globally sold games of all time was born behind the Iron Curtain on a state research computer.
extra.verification_notes: Pajitnov created Tetris in 1984 at the Dorodnitsyn Computing Center of the USSR Academy of Sciences in Moscow, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetris.

explanation: Alexey Pajitnov wrote it on an Elektronika 60 at the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow, and for years saw no royalties from the worldwide hit.

question: Pac-Man's designer said the character's shape came to him while looking at what food?
alternative_answers: a pizza with a slice missing
source_excerpt: has often claimed that the character of Pac-Man was inspired by the shape of a pizza with a missing slice

extra.why_interesting: The silhouette is instantly familiar, and once you hear the answer you can never unsee it.
extra.verification_notes: Iwatani has often said Pac-Man was inspired by a pizza with a slice missing; the 'mouth' kanji influence is a secondary account and not a food (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pac-Man).

explanation: Toru Iwatani described a pizza with one slice missing, which is exactly the yellow disc with a wedge-shaped mouth.

question: The Bluetooth logo merges two runes, the initials of a tenth-century king whose nickname the technology borrowed. Which country did he rule?
source_excerpt: The Bluetooth logo consists of a Younger Futhark bind rune for his initials, H (ᚼ) and B (ᛒ).

extra.why_interesting: A sleek modern wireless standard is secretly a Viking king's nickname, and the logo on every phone is his monogram in runes.
extra.verification_notes: Harald Bluetooth was king of Denmark (also Norway, but Denmark is his primary realm and the one tied to the Bluetooth naming story); the logo is a bind rune of his initials H and B (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_Bluetooth).

explanation: Harald Bluetooth united the Danish tribes, and the engineers picked his name hoping their standard would unite communication protocols the same way.

question: The first video ever uploaded to YouTube, in April 2005, is a 19-second clip titled 'Me at the…' what kind of place?
source_excerpt: Me at the zoo is the first video uploaded to YouTube. It was uploaded on April 23, 2005, and is 19 seconds long.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a landmark first upload to be something grand; it was a man in front of elephants saying their trunks are really long.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms 'Me at the zoo' is YouTube's first video, uploaded April 23, 2005, 19 seconds long, and still online.

explanation: Co-founder Jawed Karim filmed himself in front of the elephants at San Diego Zoo, and the clip remains online to this day.

question: Douglas Engelbart's 1964 prototype of the computer mouse had its casing made from what material?
source_excerpt: The first prototype – a one-button mouse in a wooden shell on wheels – was built in the fall of 1964 to test the concept.

extra.why_interesting: A device we think of as moulded plastic began life as a carved block that looks like a craft project.
extra.verification_notes: Engelbart's 1964 prototype mouse had a carved wooden (redwood) shell, per the Doug Engelbart Institute and widely repeated accounts; no newer development changes this.

explanation: The block was carved by hand and rolled on two perpendicular metal wheels, with a single red button on top.

question: The first-ever text message was sent to a mobile phone in Britain in December 1992. What two-word seasonal greeting did it contain?
source_excerpt: the first SMS message...sent over the Vodafone GSM network in the United Kingdom

extra.why_interesting: The month is a foothold, so the player can reason their way to a cheerful answer rather than needing to have memorised it.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Neil Papworth sent 'Merry Christmas' to Richard Jarvis on Vodafone's UK network on 3 Dec 1992; the question's wording fits this and nothing newer overturns it.

explanation: Engineer Neil Papworth typed it on a computer, since phones of the time could receive texts but had no way to send them.

question: Nintendo was founded in Kyoto in 1889, nearly a century before its first home console. What product did the company make back then?
source_excerpt: Nintendo was founded as Nintendo Koppai on 23 September 1889 by craftsman Fusajiro Yamauchi in Shimogyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a video game giant is a child of the electronics age; it predates the light bulb's mass adoption.
extra.verification_notes: Nintendo was founded in Kyoto in 1889 to make hanafuda playing cards; the first home console (Color TV-Game) came in 1977, so 'nearly a century' is fair (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo).

explanation: Fusajiro Yamauchi made hand-painted hanafuda cards, and Nintendo still sells playing cards in Japan today.

question: Three of these technology giants famously started life in a garage. Which one did not?
source_excerpt: Founded in 1975 by Bill Gates and Paul Allen to market BASIC interpreters for the Altair 8800.

extra.why_interesting: The garage origin story is so strong a Silicon Valley cliché that players assume every founding duo had one.
extra.verification_notes: Microsoft was founded in Albuquerque for the Altair 8800 (no garage), while HP, Apple and Google are the famous garage startups; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft.

explanation: Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded Microsoft in Albuquerque, New Mexico, working from an office near their first customer, while HP, Apple and Google all have celebrated garages in California.

question: Roughly how many transistors are packed onto the main processor chip of a current flagship smartphone?
source_excerpt: 19 billion transistors

extra.why_interesting: People know chips are complex but rarely grasp that a thumbnail-sized component holds more switches than there are humans on Earth.
extra.verification_notes: Flagship smartphone SoCs (e.g., Apple A17 Pro at 19 billion; A19 Pro estimated 25-30 billion) have tens of billions of transistors, so 'Billions' is correct.

explanation: Apple's A17 Pro alone holds about 19 billion transistors, more than twice the number of people on Earth, on a chip you could hide under a coin.

question: In 1991, researchers at Cambridge University pointed what is considered the world's first webcam at a shared appliance in their lab, so they could check from their desks whether a trip down the corridor was worth it. What appliance?
source_excerpt: the subject of the world's first webcam

extra.why_interesting: The ancestor of every video call existed to settle a question every office worker understands: is there any coffee left?
extra.verification_notes: The Trojan Room coffee pot at Cambridge, watched by a camera from 1991, is described as the subject of the world's first webcam; no newer events contradict this.

explanation: The Trojan Room coffee pot streamed a grainy image a few times a minute and became an early internet celebrity before it was finally switched off in 2001.

question: Before settling on Amazon, Jeff Bezos incorporated his online bookstore in 1994 under a name taken from a stage magician's incantation. What was that original name?
source_excerpt: incorporated as Cadabra, Inc. on July 5, 1994... a lawyer misheard its original name as 'cadaver'.

extra.why_interesting: The world's biggest retailer nearly launched under a name that sounded like a corpse, and the magician clue gives players a real route to it.
extra.verification_notes: Amazon was incorporated as Cadabra, Inc. on July 5, 1994 and renamed after a lawyer misheard it as 'cadaver' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Amazon); the 'abracadabra' origin is widely reported but wasn't stated on that page.

explanation: Bezos dropped it after his lawyer misheard 'Cadabra' over the phone as 'cadaver', and chose Amazon for the world's largest river instead.

question: The first-ever dot-com domain name was registered by a computer company from Massachusetts. In which year?
source_excerpt: On 15 March 1985, symbolics.com became the first (and currently, since it is still registered, the oldest) registered .com domain of the Internet.

extra.why_interesting: Players associate .com with the 1990s web boom, yet the first one predates the World Wide Web by several years.
extra.verification_notes: Symbolics (Massachusetts computer company) registered symbolics.com on 15 March 1985, the first .com domain, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Symbolics registered symbolics.com in March 1985, six years before the first website went online, and the name is still active today.

question: The default ringtone on classic Nokia phones is a few bars borrowed from a 1902 solo piece by the Spanish composer Francisco Tárrega. For which instrument was that piece written?
source_excerpt: composed in 1902 by the Spanish classical guitarist and composer Francisco Tárrega

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes the most-heard ringtone on Earth was composed by a sound designer in a Finnish lab; it is actually a 1902 classical piece, and knowing Tárrega was a guitarist is the clue that unlocks it.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Gran Vals (1902) by Tárrega is a solo guitar piece, and measures 13–16 became the Nokia tune.

explanation: The melody comes from Tárrega's 'Gran Vals', a waltz for solo guitar, which at the height of Nokia's dominance was reportedly played on phones around the world well over a billion times a day.

question: Which basilica in Barcelona has been under construction since 1882, long outliving its architect, who was killed by a tram in 1926?
source_excerpt: Glory Façade (the main entrance) remains under construction and is estimated to be completed by 2034–2035.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a major basilica is a finished historic monument; this one has been a building site for nearly a century and a half and outlived its architect by a hundred years.
extra.verification_notes: Sagrada Família began in 1882, Gaudí was killed by a tram in 1926, and the Glory Façade is still unfinished in 2026, so the claim still holds (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagrada_Fam%C3%ADlia).

explanation: Antoni Gaudí knew he would never see it finished, and work on his basilica has continued through wars, fires and funding crises ever since.

question: In 1911 a former Louvre handyman walked out of the museum with which painting, then kept it in his Paris flat for two years?
source_excerpt: hid the painting in his apartment in Paris

extra.why_interesting: The most protected painting on Earth was once simply carried out of the museum by a handyman and hidden in a flat, and that theft is a big part of why it became so famous.
extra.verification_notes: Peruggia, a former Louvre worker, stole the Mona Lisa in 1911 and hid it in his Paris apartment for about two years, per Wikipedia's Peruggia article.

explanation: Vincenzo Peruggia was caught trying to sell it in Florence, and the worldwide hunt for the missing picture turned it into the most famous painting alive.

question: Which French engineer designed the iron skeleton that holds up the Statue of Liberty from the inside?
source_excerpt: Eiffel and his structural engineer, Maurice Koechlin, decided to abandon the pier and instead build an iron truss tower.

extra.why_interesting: Players file the statue under 'America' and the engineer under 'Paris'; the surprise is that the same man holds up both icons.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia says Eiffel and his engineer Koechlin replaced Viollet-le-Duc's pier with an iron truss tower, so Eiffel is the standard answer, though Koechlin shares the credit.

explanation: Sculptor Bartholdi shaped the copper skin, but Eiffel engineered the frame inside it, a few years before his tower rose over Paris.

question: The author of The Little Prince, whose story opens with a crash in the desert, earned his living in what profession?
source_excerpt: a French writer, poet, journalist and aviator.

extra.why_interesting: The book's narrator crash-lands in the desert; players rarely realise the author really did crash in the Sahara and flew for a living.
extra.verification_notes: Saint-Exupéry was a professional aviator (airmail and military pilot), and the book opens with a pilot stranded in the desert; the only risk is that 'writer' is also a defensible answer.

explanation: Saint-Exupéry flew airmail across the Sahara and the Andes, survived a real desert crash in 1935, and vanished on a wartime flight in 1944.

question: Michelangelo's marble statue of David stands roughly how tall?
source_excerpt: With a height of 5.17 metres (17 ft 0 in), the David was not only the first colossal marble statue made in the High Renaissance

extra.why_interesting: Photos make David look like a life-size figure; in reality he towers over visitors at more than five metres.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia gives David's height as 5.17 m, so 'about 5 metres' is the only fitting option.

explanation: He is just over five metres, about three times the height of a real man, which is why visitors in Florence look so small beside him.

question: Everyone knows the Tower of Pisa leans, but what was it actually built to be?
source_excerpt: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is the campanile, or freestanding bell tower, of Pisa Cathedral.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows the tower leans; almost nobody stops to ask what the tower was for.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Leaning Tower of Pisa is the freestanding bell tower (campanile) of Pisa Cathedral; no newer developments change this.

explanation: It is the freestanding bell tower of Pisa Cathedral, and it began tilting while still under construction in the twelfth century.

question: Hokusai's famous print The Great Wave is one of a series of thirty-six views of what?
source_excerpt: The Great Wave off Kanagawa, the best known print in the series.

extra.why_interesting: The wave dominates the picture, yet it is officially a portrait of the tiny mountain in the background.
extra.verification_notes: The Great Wave is the best-known print in Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji; the series was later expanded to 46 prints but keeps its title (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty-six_Views_of_Mount_Fuji).

explanation: The mountain sits tiny in the background beneath the wave's claws, but it is the true subject of every print in the series.

question: Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper is painted directly onto the wall of a monastery dining hall in which Italian city?
source_excerpt: covers an end wall of the dining hall at the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Florence or Rome; the painting is in the dining hall of a monastery in Milan, where it has never moved.
extra.verification_notes: The Last Supper is a wall painting in the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, and it has not been moved (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Supper_(Leonardo)).

explanation: It has never left the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie, and it even survived a 1943 bombing that destroyed much of the building around it.

question: The architect who won the competition to design the Sydney Opera House came from which country?
source_excerpt: The winner, announced in Sydney on 29 January 1957, was Danish architect Jørn Utzon.

extra.why_interesting: The building is the symbol of Australia, yet it came from a Scandinavian who walked away before it opened and never saw it in person.
extra.verification_notes: Jørn Utzon, a Danish architect, won the 1957 Sydney Opera House competition, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House

explanation: Jørn Utzon quit the project in 1966 amid disputes over costs and never went back to Australia, so he never saw his finished masterpiece.

question: In which year was George Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four first published?
source_excerpt: published on 8 June 1949 in Britain by Secker & Warburg as Orwell's ninth and final completed book

extra.why_interesting: The title makes people place the book close to the 1980s; it was written in the shadow of the Second World War, when 1984 was a distant future.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms first publication on 8 June 1949 by Secker & Warburg (UK), with the US edition following in June 1949.

explanation: Orwell finished it on a remote Scottish island while gravely ill and died only months after it came out, a full thirty-five years before the year in its title.

question: Which of these famous works is NOT in the Louvre in Paris?
source_excerpt: The Winged Victory of Samothrace stands at the top of the Daru staircase

extra.why_interesting: All four are world-famous European masterpieces of the kind people associate with the Louvre; only someone who knows where Rembrandt's giant canvas lives can pick it out.
extra.verification_notes: The Night Watch is Rembrandt's painting in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. The other three are permanent Louvre holdings, per https://collections.louvre.fr/en/ark:/53355/cl010277627 (Venus de Milo) and https://www.louvre.fr/en/explore/the-palace/a-stairway-to-victory (Winged Victory).

explanation: The Night Watch is Rembrandt's pride of the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam; the other three are among the Louvre's biggest crowd-pullers.

question: Almost two thousand years after it was built, which building in Rome still holds the record for the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome?
source_excerpt: Almost two thousand years after it was built, the Pantheon's dome is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume concrete records belong to modern engineering; a building from the second century still holds this one.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Pantheon's dome is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, and I found no newer claim that overtakes it (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome).

explanation: Roman builders lightened the concrete toward the top and left a nine-metre hole in the middle, and nobody has beaten the span without steel since.

question: In 1613 Shakespeare's Globe Theatre burned to the ground after its thatched roof was set alight by what piece of stage equipment, fired during a play?
source_excerpt: A theatrical cannon, set off during the performance, misfired, igniting the wooden beams and thatching.

extra.why_interesting: The idea of firing a real cannon inside a wooden, straw-roofed theatre sounds absurd today, which is exactly why the answer lands.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms a cannon fired during Henry VIII on 29 June 1613 ignited the thatched roof.

explanation: The cannon was fired for a royal entrance in Henry the Eighth, a spark caught the thatch, and the theatre was gone within an hour, reportedly with no deaths.

question: Rodin's famous statue The Thinker was first designed to sit above a monumental pair of doors, gazing down at scenes from an epic poem about hell. Which poet was the figure originally meant to represent?
source_excerpt: The Thinker was initially named The Poet (French: Le Poète), and was part of a large commission begun in 1880.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume The Thinker is an anonymous everyman deep in thought; in fact he is a portrait of a specific medieval poet, brooding over his own vision of hell.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms The Thinker was designed for The Gates of Hell, originally titled The Poet, and is conventionally identified as Dante; a minor scholarly dispute exists but does not make another answer defensible.

explanation: The figure was created for Rodin's The Gates of Hell, inspired by the Divine Comedy, and was originally titled The Poet before the world renamed it The Thinker.

question: The Leaning Tower of Pisa began to tilt while it was still being built. Roughly how long did its construction take, from the first stone to completion?
source_excerpt: On 9 August 1173, the foundations of the tower were laid. ... The bell-chamber was added in 1372.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture a medieval tower going up in a decade or two; the real build dragged on for almost two centuries, and the pauses are part of why the tower is still standing.
extra.verification_notes: Construction ran from 1173 to 1372 (about 199 years), so 'Over 150 years' is correct; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaning_Tower_of_Pisa

explanation: Work started in 1173 and finished in 1372, nearly two hundred years later, with long pauses for wars that let the soft soil settle and probably saved the tower from collapse.

question: The fiery green paste served with sushi in most restaurants around the world is not real wasabi but mainly which cheaper root, dyed green?
topic: Food, drink and cooking around the world
source_excerpt: A common substitute is a mixture of horseradish, mustard, starch, and green food coloring or spinach powder.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the green paste on their sushi plate is a Japanese root; it is almost always a cheaper European one in disguise.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Wasabi article confirms that horseradish (with mustard and green colouring) is the standard substitute at most sushi restaurants outside Japan.

explanation: Real wasabi is costly and loses its punch within minutes of grating, so most restaurants serve horseradish with mustard and green colouring instead.

question: In 1667 the Dutch let the English keep Manhattan while they held on to a tiny Indonesian island that was then the world's only source of which spice?
topic: Food, drink and cooking around the world
source_excerpt: the English kept the island of Manhattan... In return, Run was formally abandoned to the Dutch.

extra.why_interesting: Manhattan today is priceless, yet in 1667 the Dutch were content to let it go to keep a nutmeg island a few kilometres long. The spice trade framing lets a player work through the famous spices to the right one.
extra.verification_notes: Treaty of Breda 1667 let England keep Manhattan while the Dutch kept nutmeg-producing Run (Banda Islands), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run_Island.

explanation: The island of Run in the Banda Islands grew the only nutmeg on Earth, and at the time a sack of it was worth far more than a swampy trading post called New Amsterdam.

question: Despite its name, the pineapple-and-ham Hawaiian pizza was invented in 1962 in which country?
topic: Food, drink and cooking around the world
source_excerpt: Sam Panopoulos, a Greek-born Canadian, is credited with creating the first Hawaiian pizza at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham-Kent, Ontario, Canada, in 1962.

extra.why_interesting: The name points to the Pacific and the toppings point to Italy, yet the dish was born in a small Ontario town.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia credits Sam Panopoulos with creating Hawaiian pizza in 1962 at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham-Kent, Ontario, Canada; I found no contradicting source, though I checked only this one.

explanation: Greek immigrant Sam Panopoulos first put tinned pineapple on a pizza at his restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, and named it after the brand on the tin.

question: Walnuts, pistachios and peanuts are sold in their shells, but one popular nut never is, because its shell contains a caustic oil related to poison ivy. Which nut?
topic: Food, drink and cooking around the world
source_excerpt: Because it can cause dermatitis, cashews are typically not sold in the shell to consumers.

extra.why_interesting: Players have cracked walnuts, almonds and pistachios but never once seen this nut in its shell, and never asked why.
extra.verification_notes: Cashew shells contain anacardic acid, related to poison ivy's urushiol, and cashews are not sold in the shell to consumers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cashew).

explanation: The cashew shell is laced with anacardic acid, a skin-blistering relative of poison ivy's toxin, so the nuts are shelled and heat-treated before they reach any shop.

question: Long before anyone put tomatoes in it, the Asian sauce that gave ketchup its name was made by fermenting what?
topic: Food, drink and cooking around the world
source_excerpt: it meant the brine of pickled fish or shellfish.

extra.why_interesting: The world's most familiar tomato sauce began life with no tomatoes at all, as something closer to Vietnamese fish sauce.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Ketchup article says the original Hokkien ke-tsiap meant the brine of pickled fish or shellfish, so fermented fish is correct.

explanation: Ketchup started as a salty fermented fish sauce in Southeast Asia, and the British made mushroom and walnut versions before tomatoes took over in the 1800s.

question: It is not Britain and it is not China. Which country drinks the most tea per person in the world?
topic: Food, drink and cooking around the world
source_excerpt: As of 2025, Turkey still leads the global consumption.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone reaches for Britain or China, but the real answer is a country where tea is drunk from tulip-shaped glasses all day long. The stem rules out the two reflex answers so the player has to think about where tea culture is strongest.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's per-capita tea consumption list ranks Turkey first (3.16 kg), ahead of Ireland, and says it still led as of 2025; the underlying data is from 2016.

explanation: Turks drink around three kilograms of tea per person each year, roughly twice the British figure, mostly black tea from small tulip-shaped glasses.

question: Which spiky Southeast Asian fruit is banned on Singapore's metro trains because of its overpowering smell?
topic: Food, drink and cooking around the world
source_excerpt: The fruit's strong smell has led to its ban from public transport systems in Singapore and in Bangkok.

extra.why_interesting: A fruit so smelly that a modern city has signage banning it from trains, yet locals adore it.
extra.verification_notes: Durian is banned on Singapore MRT trains due to its smell (since 1988), per Wikipedia and https://mothership.sg/2025/05/singapore-ban-durians-hotels-public-transport/; no evidence of change.

explanation: Durian is prized across Southeast Asia for its custardy flesh, but the smell is so strong that Singapore's transit signs show it crossed out next to cigarettes.

question: Tempura, the light battered and deep-fried dish, was introduced to Japan in the 1500s by missionaries and traders from which European country?
topic: Food, drink and cooking around the world
source_excerpt: toward the end of the 16th century, the technique of fritter-cooking with a batter of flour and eggs was acquired in Nagasaki from Portuguese missionaries.

extra.why_interesting: Tempura feels as Japanese as sushi, but the batter-frying technique came off a European ship. A player who knows the Portuguese were the first Europeans in Japan can get there by reasoning.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Portuguese missionaries introduced the batter-frying technique to Nagasaki in the late 16th century; no dispute or newer development found.

explanation: Portuguese sailors fried fish and vegetables in batter on fasting days, and the Japanese adopted and refined the technique into tempura.

question: Authentic Scottish haggis has been illegal to import into the United States since 1971 because the recipe includes which sheep organ?
topic: Food, drink and cooking around the world
source_excerpt: a ban on food containing sheep lung, which constitutes 10–15% of the traditional recipe

extra.why_interesting: A national dish that is a crime to import into America, not for safety scares but for one specific organ in the recipe. A player who knows haggis is made from sheep offal can work down the list of organs.
extra.verification_notes: The USDA has barred livestock lungs as human food since 1971, which blocks traditional sheep-lung haggis; Wikipedia says the ban persists after the 2022 lamb-import change.

explanation: US food rules forbid lungs in anything sold to eat, so Scottish producers make a lung-free version for the American market.

question: Which country produces the most olive oil in the world, usually around half of the global total?
topic: Food, drink and cooking around the world
source_excerpt: In 2022, Spain was the world's largest producer, manufacturing 24% of the world's total.

extra.why_interesting: Marketing has trained everyone to picture Tuscany, but the bottle labelled Italian is often filled with oil pressed in Andalusia.
extra.verification_notes: Spain is consistently the top olive oil producer (about 24–45% of world output depending on harvest); the 'around half' phrasing is loose but the answer is unambiguous. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olive_oil

explanation: Spain out-produces Italy several times over, and a great deal of Spanish oil is shipped to Italy to be bottled under Italian labels.

question: True or false: Marco Polo brought pasta to Italy after discovering noodles in China.
topic: Food, drink and cooking around the world
source_excerpt: The popular belief that Marco Polo introduced pasta to Italy from China to Italy is considered a myth by many historians.

extra.why_interesting: This is one of the most repeated food legends in the world, and a dated legal document quietly disproves it.
extra.verification_notes: Marco Polo bringing pasta to Italy is a widely debunked myth; pasta was already made in Sicily by 1154 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_pasta).

explanation: A notary in Genoa recorded a basket of dried pasta in an estate in 1279, well before Marco Polo came home in 1295, so Italians were already eating it.

question: Gram for gram, which of these contains more sugar: tomato ketchup or classic Coca-Cola?
topic: Food, drink and cooking around the world
source_excerpt: Heinz Tomato Ketchup contains 23.7g of sugar per 100g

extra.why_interesting: Cola is the poster child for sugar, so players confidently pick it, but gram for gram the savoury-looking condiment has roughly twice as much.
extra.verification_notes: Heinz ketchup has ~23-24 g sugar per 100 g versus Coca-Cola ~10.6 g per 100 ml (about 10 g per 100 g), so ketchup has more sugar gram for gram.

explanation: Ketchup carries around 22 grams of sugar per 100 grams, about double the roughly 11 grams in the same amount of Coca-Cola, you just eat far less of it.

question: Three of these spices have been grown in Asia for thousands of years. One of them did not exist anywhere in Asia until European ships brought it in the 1500s. Which one?
topic: Food, drink and cooking around the world
source_excerpt: The Portuguese introduced them first to Africa and Arabia, and then to their colonies and trading posts in Asia, including Goa, Sri Lanka, and Malacca.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the fire in Indian, Thai and Sichuan food has always been there; in fact the chili only arrived by European ship a few centuries ago, making it the youngest ingredient in those ancient cuisines.
extra.verification_notes: Chili peppers are native to the Americas and were introduced to Asia by the Portuguese in the 16th century, while black pepper, ginger and cardamom are native to Asia.

explanation: The chili pepper is a native of the Americas, so Indian, Thai and Sichuan cooking had no chili heat at all until Portuguese and Spanish traders carried the plant across the oceans.

question: The grey writing core of a pencil and the stone in a diamond ring are both pure forms of the same element. Which one?
source_excerpt: Graphite is a crystalline allotrope (form) of the element carbon.

extra.why_interesting: A soft grey smudge and the hardest gem on Earth seem like opposites, yet they are the same single element arranged differently.
extra.verification_notes: Graphite and diamond are both allotropes of carbon; the clay in real pencil cores is a minor quibble that doesn't change the answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphite).

explanation: In graphite the carbon atoms sit in slippery sheets that slide off onto paper, while in diamond every atom is locked to four neighbours in a rigid lattice.

question: You hold a helium balloon on a string inside a car with the windows shut. The driver accelerates hard. Which way does the balloon lean?
source_excerpt: When you accelerate your car forwards, the air within your vehicle sloshes backwards, creating a buoyant force now pushing the helium balloon towards the front of the vehicle.

extra.why_interesting: Every loose object in a car lurches backward when you floor it, so players confidently say 'backward' and are stunned that the balloon does the opposite.
extra.verification_notes: Air sloshes backward during forward acceleration, creating a pressure gradient that pushes the buoyant helium balloon forward, per https://www.iflscience.com/you-have-a-helium-balloon-in-your-car-what-direction-does-it-go-when-you-accelerate-78598

explanation: The air in the cabin is heavier than the balloon and piles up toward the back, so the buoyant balloon gets pushed the other way, just as it floats up away from heavier air.

question: Of all the gas you breathe out with each exhale, which single gas makes up the largest share?
source_excerpt: Exhaled air consists of 78 percent nitrogen, 16 percent oxygen, 4 percent carbon dioxide and potentially thousands of other compounds.

extra.why_interesting: School teaches 'breathe in oxygen, breathe out carbon dioxide', so players answer carbon dioxide, when in fact the breath you exhale is still overwhelmingly the gas you never used at all.
